title: In the Age of AI Knowledge Matters More Not Less
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman identifies an internal contradiction in AFT President Randi Weingarten's AI-in-education speech, which simultaneously called for more project-based learning AND stronger foundational literacy, numeracy, and civic knowledge -- ideas that are in tension, not complementary. Aldeman argues that the progressive education argument ('facts are cheap, look them up') has been taken to its logical extreme by AI, which can now look up everything instantly -- and this actually makes foundational knowledge more important, not less. Drawing on Willingham's 2020 research in the AFT's own publication, Aldeman argues that domain knowledge is what enables critical thinking: abstract critical-thinking skills disconnected from content knowledge cannot substitute for actual fluency. The students who will benefit most from AI are those who know enough to ask good questions, evaluate answers, and build on what they learn -- not those who know the least.
points: The progressive argument 'students don't need to memorize facts because they can look them up' has been taken to its logical extreme by AI -- but rather than making knowledge less important, this raises the bar: you now need to know enough to prompt well, evaluate AI output, and build on it.

Critical thinking is not a free-floating skill: domain knowledge is what enables it, as Willingham argues in the AFT's own publication -- teaching abstract critical-thinking divorced from content knowledge risks de-emphasizing the very thing that makes critical thinking possible.

Project-based learning can be valuable when students already possess a strong knowledge foundation; when schools use projects as a substitute for content rather than an application of it, students spend lots of time doing activities without really learning very much.
The students who will benefit most from AI are not the ones who know the least but the ones who know enough to ask good questions, evaluate the answers, and proceed to build on what they learn.

Weingarten's speech contains a tension she does not acknowledge: redesigning schooling around projects and experiences is in direct conflict with ensuring students have a solid foundation in literacy, numeracy, and civic engagement.
quotes: For decades, progressive education reformers like Weingarten have argued that schools spend too much time on facts and 'rote' memorization and not enough on projects, experiences, and real-world applications.

Artificial intelligence has taken that logic even further. Students can now ask a chatbot to explain a concept, summarize a book, or draft an essay in seconds. But that's precisely why foundational knowledge has become more important, not less.

'Domain knowledge is a crucial driver of thinking skill,' wrote University of Virginia cognitive psychologist Daniel Willingham in 2020 for the American Educator, a publication of the American Federation of Teachers. 'Critical thinking for open-ended problems is enabled by extensive stores of knowledge.'

Project-based learning can be valuable when students already possess a strong foundation of knowledge and skills. Too often, however, schools treat projects as a substitute for content rather than an opportunity to apply content.

The students who will benefit most from AI won't be the ones who know the least. It will be the ones who know enough to ask good questions, evaluate the answers, and then proceed to build on what they learn.
